# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

Infer the repo from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

display.text:
# Workspace User Management

The nonprofit's onboarding, self-service, and administration of its Google Workspace users and groups.

## Language

**Applicant**:
A person requesting a Workspace account who has not yet received one through onboarding.
_Avoid_: User, pending user

**Signup request**:
An applicant's submitted information awaiting an administrator's acceptance or rejection.
_Avoid_: Account, pending user

**Workspace user**:
A person with a managed Google account in the nonprofit's Workspace organization.
_Avoid_: Applicant

**Administrator**:
A Workspace user whose Google Workspace administrative privileges authorize the relevant management action.
_Avoid_: App administrator

**Contact email**:
An email address used to contact a person, distinct from their managed Workspace email address.

**Workspace email**:
The primary email address of a person's managed Google Workspace account.

**Self-service**:
A Workspace user's submission of changes to their own contact information for administrator approval.

**Profile change request**:
A Workspace user's proposed contact email or phone changes awaiting approval together by an administrator with sufficient privileges. Each user has at most one pending request; a new submission replaces it.
_Avoid_: Profile update

**Account handover**:
Delivery of first-login access to an approved applicant after their Workspace account has been created.

**Suspension**:
Reversible deactivation of a Workspace account that retains the account and its data.
_Avoid_: Deletion, deactivation

**Deletion**:
Removal of a Workspace account after the organization has resolved the disposition of its data.
_Avoid_: Suspension, deactivation

**Group**:
A Google Group within the nonprofit's Workspace organization.

**Group membership**:
A Workspace user's relationship to a group, with a member, manager, or owner role.

**Group manager**:
A group member with Google's manager role in that group; this role does not itself confer application administrator authority.

**Group owner**:
A group member with Google's owner role in that group; this role does not itself confer application administrator authority.

**Initial group membership**:
A group membership explicitly selected by the reviewing administrator during onboarding, with no automatic assignments. Its role is member unless manager or owner is explicitly selected.

1: # Use administrator OAuth and approved profile changes
2: 
3: Ordinary-user OAuth consent does not authorize Directory profile writes, even to the user's own account. For this small nonprofit, users submit verified contact email and phone changes for approval; the application executes approved changes and administrative operations using the acting administrator's OAuth credentials. Google therefore enforces that administrator's privileges and resource restrictions, without a shared stronger account or a parallel application role model.
4: 
5: Prefer this workflow over domain-wide delegation: Google's Directory user write scope is not limited to contact fields, and delegation scopes do not restrict which account a service account may impersonate. The trade-off is that contact changes wait for an authorized administrator instead of taking effect immediately. Domain-wide delegation can be reconsidered if that approval delay becomes unacceptable.
6: 
7: Request `admin.directory.user` for user management and `admin.directory.group` for group and membership management; add read-only role inspection only if required for the interface. Restrict profile change requests to contact email and phone, preserve unrelated Directory entries, and keep Workspace email, account recovery fields, and security settings outside that workflow. A new contact email must be verified before it can be approved. Do not retry denied operations using stronger credentials.
8: 
9: Send verification, outcome, and administrator notification emails through a dedicated Workspace mailbox with a separate offline OAuth grant limited to `gmail.send`. Notify a configured Google Group when a verified signup or profile change request is submitted, including a review-queue link and minimal personal information. The notification group's membership determines delivery only, never approval authority; configure it to accept mail from the sender.
10: 
11: Assume administrator-managed Directory/contact sharing is enabled and managed users are visible in the Directory. Read the signed-in user's own profile with their OAuth grant containing `admin.directory.user.readonly`, explicitly using `viewType=domain_public`. Resolve the target from the authenticated identity and return only that user's permitted shared fields. Omitted contact fields are unavailable, not evidence that the stored value is empty. Keep credentials server-side; no shared reader account, delegated Users Read role, or private/admin-view fallback is required. Administrative reads and approved writes still use the acting administrator's grant.
12: 
13: Require a successful current own-profile lookup for protected access; unavailable/hidden/deleted profiles or rejected credentials deny access with an explicit unavailable or reconnection outcome. This is a visibility/access check, not an administrator-only `suspended` status check. Verify suspended/deleted-account behavior with existing sessions in the live tenant; access denial depends on Google's credential and Directory propagation and must not be described as instantaneous suspension detection.
14: 
15: References: [Directory user permissions](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users#retrieve_a_user_as_a_non-administrator), [Directory read views](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get), [OAuth scopes](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/authorizing), [domain-wide delegation guidance](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/apps/domain-wide-delegation-best-practices), and [existing-user password reset](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/reset-a-users-password).

(End of file - total 15 lines)
</content>

Domain-wide delegation can be reconsidered if that approval delay becomes unacceptable.

Request `admin.directory.user` for user management and `admin.directory.group` for group and membership management; add read-only role inspection only if required for the interface. Restrict profile change requests to contact email and phone, preserve unrelated Directory entries, and keep Workspace email, account recovery fields, and security settings outside that workflow. A new contact email must be verified before it can be approved. Do not retry denied operations using stronger credentials.

Send verification, outcome, and administrator notification emails through a dedicated Workspace mailbox with a separate offline OAuth grant limited to `gmail.send`. Notify a configured Google Group when a verified signup or profile change request is submitted, including a review-queue link and minimal personal information. The notification group's membership determines delivery only, never approval authority; configure it to accept mail from the sender.

Assume administrator-managed Directory/contact sharing is enabled and managed users are visible in the Directory. Read the signed-in user's own profile with their OAuth grant containing `admin.directory.user.readonly`, explicitly using `viewType=domain_public`. Resolve the target from the authenticated identity and return only that user's permitted shared fields. Omitted contact fields are unavailable, not evidence that the stored value is empty. Keep credentials server-side; no shared reader account, delegated Users Read role, or private/admin-view fallback is required. Administrative reads and approved writes still use the acting administrator's grant.

Require a successful current own-profile lookup for protected access; unavailable/hidden/deleted profiles or rejected credentials deny access with an explicit unavailable or reconnection outcome. This is a visibility/access check, not an administrator-only `suspended` status check. Verify suspended/deleted-account behavior with existing sessions in the live tenant; access denial depends on Google's credential and Directory propagation and must not be described as instantaneous suspension detection.

References: [Directory user permissions](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/manage-users#retrieve_a_user_as_a_non-administrator), [Directory read views](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users/get), [OAuth scopes](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/authorizing), [domain-wide delegation guidance](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/apps/domain-wide-delegation-best-practices), and [existing-user password reset](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/users/reset-a-users-password).

{"body":"## Problem Statement

The nonprofit needs a simpler way to onboard people, maintain their Google Workspace information, and offboard departing users. Today, this work requires administrators to coordinate requests and perform management through Google's tools, while ordinary users lack a suitable place to request changes to their own contact information.

The application must not introduce a second authoritative user directory or a conflicting permission system. Applicants need to request accounts before they have managed Google identities; existing Workspace users must see only their own information; administrators must act within their actual Google privileges. The organization is small, so operating cost and administrative effort must remain low.

The codebase currently provides a Next.js application scaffold and a configured shadcn/Tailwind UI. Drizzle and Neon dependencies are installed, but authentication, persistence, Workspace integrations, workflows, and application tests are not implemented.

## Solution

Provide one application for the nonprofit's Workspace organization, with public email-verified signup, Google-backed sign-in for existing Workspace users, administrator review queues, user and group administration, and suspension-first offboarding.

Applicants submit a signup request without needing a personal Google account. An administrator reviews it, confirms a programmatically generated Workspace email suggestion, and accepts or rejects it. Acceptance creates the managed account and explicitly selected group memberships. Account handover uses Google's existing-user password-reset email flow in the Admin console. Rejected requests are deleted after outcome notification.

Workspace users view their own Google-authoritative profile and submit contact email or phone changes for approval. An administrator approves the reviewed request and the application writes to Google using that administrator's OAuth credentials. This preserves Google's permission enforcement without domain-wide delegation or application-owned administrator roles.

Administrators manage users and Google Groups within their Google privileges, including member, manager, and owner memberships. Suspension is the normal offboarding action; deletion is separate and requires confirmation that data disposition was resolved in Google's Admin console.

Verification, outcome, and review-notification emails use a dedicated Workspace mailbox. Deploy on Vercel with Neon Free Postgres for application-owned workflow data, keeping the architecture inexpensive and leaving provider tier management to the organization.

## User Stories

### Applicants and onboarding

1. As an applicant, I want to request a Workspace account without already having one, so that I can join the organization.
2. As an applicant, I want to apply without needing a personal Google account, so that account eligibility does not depend on my choice of email provider.
3. As an applicant, I want to provide my given name, family name, and contact email, so that an administrator has the required information to review my signup request.
4. As an applicant, I want to provide an optional phone number, so that the organization can contact me through an additional channel if needed.
5. As an applicant, I want clear validation feedback, so that I can correct missing or invalid information before submission.
6. As an applicant, I want to verify my contact email, so that the organization knows I can receive account-related messages there.
7. As an applicant, I want confirmation that my verified signup request was submitted, so that I know it is awaiting administrator review.
8. As an applicant, I want the organization to assign my Workspace email, so that account addresses follow its conventions rather than applicant preferences.
9. As an applicant, I want an email outcome for my signup request, so that I know whether I have been accepted or rejected without an applicant dashboard.
10. As an approved applicant, I want a Google-generated password-reset link at an address I can already access, so that I can obtain access to my new account without receiving a plaintext password.
11. As an approved applicant, I want to choose a new password during account handover, so that my ongoing access does not depend on a temporary provisioning password.
12. As a rejected applicant, I want my submitted profile deleted after outcome notification, so that the application does not retain unnecessary applicant information.

### Administrator review and provisioning

13. As an administrator, I want a review queue of verified signup requests, so that I can evaluate applicants in one place.
14. As an administrator, I want an email notification when a verified signup request is submitted, so that I do not have to discover new requests by repeatedly checking the application.
15. As an administrator, I want to view the information submitted by an applicant, so that I can decide whether to accept the signup request.
16. As an administrator, I want a programmatically generated Workspace email suggestion, so that creating an account requires less manual work.
17. As an administrator, I want to confirm or edit the generated suggestion and check its availability, so that the resulting Workspace address is appropriate and does not conflict with an existing account.
18. As an administrator, I want acceptance to create the user in Google Workspace, so that approval results in a managed account rather than a separate application-only user.
19. As an administrator, I want to reject a signup request and notify the applicant, so that unsuitable requests can be resolved and their submitted data removed.
20. As an administrator, I want to select optional initial groups explicitly, so that new users receive only intended memberships.
21. As an administrator, I want initial memberships to default to member, so that management authority is not granted accidentally.
22. As an administrator, I want to select manager or owner roles explicitly when authorized, so that onboarding can establish the intended group responsibilities.
23. As an administrator, I want to distinguish account creation, membership assignment, and account handover completion, so that I can finish partially completed onboarding correctly.
24. As an administrator, I want failed provisioning to remain recoverable, so that temporary Google or database failures do not lose an accepted applicant's request.
25. As an administrator, I want repeated approval or retry attempts not to create duplicate accounts, so that recovery is safe.
26. As an administrator, I want an email collision never to attach an applicant to an existing account, so that an applicant cannot receive someone else's identity.
27. As an administrator, I want unreviewed signup requests to expire after 30 days, so that the review queue does not retain obsolete applications indefinitely.
28. As an administrator, I want successful applicant form data removed after provisioning and handover, so that only the minimal provisioning record remains.

### Workspace user self-service

29. As a Workspace user, I want to sign in with my managed Google identity, so that I do not need another password or application account.
30. As a Workspace user, I want my displayed profile to come from Google Workspace, so that changes made through Google's tools are reflected rather than contradicted by an application copy.
31. As a Workspace user, I want to see only my own permitted profile and request, so that other users' information remains private.
32. As a Workspace user, I want to propose a contact email change, so that the organization can reach me at the right address.
33. As a Workspace user, I want to verify a replacement contact email, so that an administrator can approve a reachable address.
34. As a Workspace user, I want to propose a contact phone change, so that the organization can maintain accurate contact information.
35. As a Workspace user, I want to see my pending profile change request separately from my current profile, so that I understand which values are proposed and which are already authoritative in Google.
36. As a Workspace user, I want a newer submission to replace my one pending request, so that an administrator reviews my latest intended changes.
37. As a Workspace user, I want an email outcome for my profile change request, so that I know whether the changes were accepted or rejected.
38. As a Workspace user, I want rejection to leave my Google profile unchanged, so that unapproved proposals cannot alter my account.
39. As a Workspace user, I want my application access to stop after my account is suspended or deleted, so that application sessions do not bypass Workspace account status.

### Profile approval and permission enforcement

40. As an administrator, I want to review pending profile change requests, so that contact changes can be approved without giving ordinary users Directory write authority.
41. As an administrator, I want an email notification when a verified profile change request is submitted, so that I can respond without continuous polling.
42. As an administrator, I want to approve or reject the entire reviewed request, so that the outcome is unambiguous.
43. As an administrator, I want approval to apply only the request version I reviewed, so that a concurrent replacement cannot change what I authorize.
44. As an administrator, I want approved changes to preserve unrelated Google contact entries and recovery settings, so that updating contact information does not damage other account data.
45. As an administrator, I want management operations to execute under my Google OAuth credentials, so that Google enforces my privileges and resource restrictions.
46. As an administrator, I want permission denials to be reported without escalation to another account, so that the application cannot bypass Google's authorization decisions.
47. As an administrator, I want Google-side role changes to affect application permissions, so that the application does not retain stale administrator authority.

### User administration and offboarding

48. As an administrator, I want to list Workspace users within my authorized scope, so that I can find the accounts I manage.
49. As an administrator, I want to view and edit Google-supported user information within my privileges, so that I can manage fields that ordinary users cannot change.
50. As an administrator, I want to suspend a Workspace user, so that I can stop access while retaining the account and its data.
51. As an administrator, I want to unsuspend a Workspace user when authorized, so that reversible offboarding can be undone.
52. As an administrator, I want deletion to be a distinct, explicitly confirmed action after data disposition, so that permanent removal does not happen accidentally or before the organization has dealt with the user's data.

### Group administration

53. As an administrator, I want to list Google Groups, so that I can find the groups I am authorized to manage.
54. As an administrator, I want to create a group and edit its basic details, so that the organization's group structure stays useful.
55. As an administrator, I want to delete a group when authorized, so that obsolete groups can be removed.
56. As an administrator, I want to inspect direct group memberships, so that I can understand who belongs to each group and in which role.
57. As an administrator, I want to add or remove direct Workspace-user memberships, so that group access and mailing-list membership match organizational needs.
58. As an administrator, I want to assign and change member, manager, and owner roles, so that group responsibilities are managed explicitly.
59. As an administrator, I want unrelated existing group settings preserved, so that basic management does not unexpectedly change posting or privacy behavior.
60. As an organization operator, I want group owner/manager roles and notification-group membership not to grant application-wide administrator authority, so that authorization remains tied to Google administrative privileges.

### Operations, privacy, and usability

61. As an organization operator, I want emails sent through a dedicated Workspace mailbox, so that notifications use an organization-controlled identity with send-only permission.
62. As an organization operator, I want review notifications delivered to one configured Google Group, so that recipients can be managed through Google without an application role system.
63. As an organization operator, I want notification emails to contain minimal personal information and a review link, so that submitted profiles and secrets are not distributed unnecessarily.
64. As an organization operator, I want email failures to be visible and safely retryable, so that requests and outcomes do not disappear silently.
65. As an organization operator, I want OAuth connections to report revocation or reconnection needs, so that failed credentials can be repaired without silently changing the acting identity.
66. As an organization operator, I want workflow records separated from Google-authoritative profiles, so that the application does not create a second directory or permission system.
67. As an organization operator, I want serverless hosting and a database that can become idle, so that a small workload has low ongoing cost.
68. As an organization operator, I want provider tier management handled manually, so that the application does not introduce billing features or automatic upgrades.
69. As an organization operator, I want public submissions and verification emails protected against invalid input and abuse, so that avoidable misuse does not consume limited resources.
70. As an applicant or Workspace user, I want accessible forms and clear loading, success, and error states, so that I can complete workflows using the existing consistent UI.

## Implementation Decisions

### Domain and module interfaces

- Preserve the agreed vocabulary: applicant, signup request, Workspace user, administrator, contact email, Workspace email, profile change request, account handover, suspension, deletion, group, group membership, group manager, group owner, and initial group membership.
- Support one Workspace organization. A personal Google account used elsewhere is not the applicant's new managed identity.
- Extend the existing application with public signup, own-profile self-service, administrator review, user administration, and group administration. Expose their behavior through the running application's browser-facing interface rather than inventing a separate public management API.
- Keep request handling, authorization, persistence, and Google operations behind that application interface. Reuse existing patterns and installed dependencies; do not create one-to-one pass-through modules or speculative abstractions.
- Trust-boundary contracts validate inputs, authenticated identity, ownership, current authority, request version, and completion state on the server. Browser-provided identifiers never establish ownership or privileges.

### Identity and Google access

- Existing Workspace users authenticate through Google. Validate token signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and applicable state/nonce protections; enforce organizational membership from verified identity claims, not an email suffix or sign-in UI hint.
- Bind the authenticated identity to a stable Google Directory user identifier server-side. Handle primary-email changes safely. Do not assume undocumented equality between the OpenID Connect subject and the Directory user identifier.
- Re-evaluate account status for protected access so suspension or deletion cannot be bypassed by a previously issued application session. Google-side privilege changes must also be respected.
- Ordinary-user consent does not authorize Directory writes. Self-service therefore submits approval requests rather than writing directly to Google.
- Use the acting administrator's OAuth connection for administrative reads and writes. Google enforces that account's action, resource, and organizational-unit restrictions. Do not use a stronger shared writer, infer authority from broad administrator flags alone, or retry a denial under another identity.
- Request the user-management and group-management Directory scopes required by the selected operations. Add read-only role inspection only when the interface needs it and the calling account is authorized. If roles are interpreted, account for indirect assignments, privilege hierarchy, and assignment scope.
- Ordinary-user Directory reads expose domain-public information and do not document a full own-profile exception. Provide private own-profile display through an isolated backend OAuth reader with the Directory user read-only scope and a delegated account limited to Users Read in relevant organizational units. Derive the target from the authenticated session and return only permitted own-profile fields. This reader performs no writes and does not expand administrator listings beyond the acting administrator's scope.
- Keep reader, acting-administrator, and notification-sender grants isolated by purpose, including protection against accidentally accumulating write grants on the reader. Credentials remain server-side and protected; revoked or expired connections have explicit reconnection behavior.
- Do not use domain-wide delegation initially. This avoids its broad impersonation authority while accepting administrator approval delays for contact changes.

### Signup, approval, and account handover

- Require given name, family name, and verified contact email; phone is optional. Email verification precedes entry into the review queue. There is no applicant login/dashboard.
- Generate Workspace email suggestions using the agreed given.family convention. The reviewing administrator confirms or edits them; applicants have no address-selection interface. Validate suggestions against Google naming rules and availability without connecting a collision to an existing user.
- Acceptance provisions through Google under the approving administrator's authority. Initial group memberships are optional and explicit, with member as the default and manager/owner as deliberate selections.
- Generate a random temporary password only for the Google creation operation, require a password change, and do not retain or expose that password in workflow records, logs, or emails.
- Account handover remains a manual Google Admin console operation: reset the existing user's password with required change enabled and email Google's reset link to an address the applicant can access. Track handover completion before purging successful applicant form data.
- Distinguish account creation, initial membership completion, and account handover so failures can be recovered without repeating completed work or creating another account.
- Reject stale or already-resolved review actions. Preserve sufficient progress to recover when an external operation succeeds but later database or notification work fails; do not claim a distributed atomic transaction across Google and Postgres.
- Rejected requests are deleted after outcome notification. Unreviewed signup requests expire after 30 days. Successful applicant form data is removed after provisioning and handover; retain only a minimal provisioning record identifying the Google account and approving administrator.

### Profile change requests

- Users may propose contact email and phone changes only. Name, Workspace email, organizational assignments, memberships, account status, recovery fields, and security settings remain administrator-controlled.
- Store proposals separately from the current Google profile. Verify a replacement contact email before approval; replacing it requires verification of the new proposal.
- Allow at most one pending profile change request per Workspace user. A new submission replaces it. Enforce this constraint in persistence, not just the interface.
- Approval/rejection applies to the whole reviewed request. Use request-version/concurrency protection so a replaced proposal cannot be approved with stale reviewed contents.
- Approved values are written with the approving administrator's OAuth credentials. Contact email and phone belong in Google contact arrays, not the Workspace primary address or account-recovery fields.
- Preserve unrelated contact-array entries when submitting complete desired arrays to Google. Show success only after the relevant Google write succeeds; rejection leaves the profile unchanged.
- Notification failure after a successful write must not cause the write to be repeated as if it had failed.

### User and group administration

- Provide authorized user listing, profile editing, suspension, unsuspension, and deletion. Permission checks apply to each action and target, not merely access to an administrator screen.
- Suspension is the standard offboarding action. Deletion requires distinct confirmation that data disposition has been resolved manually in Google's Admin console. Do not implement automated data transfer.
- Provide basic Google Group listing, creation, detail editing, and deletion, plus direct membership inspection, addition, removal, and member/manager/owner role changes for Workspace users.
- Preserve unrelated existing group settings. Group owner/manager roles do not automatically confer application administrator authority.
- Paginate Google lists correctly. Treat Google permissions, propagation delays, resource conflicts, and missing records as actual external outcomes rather than silently bypassing them.

### Persistence and recovery

- Use Drizzle ORM with Neon Postgres for signup requests, email-verification evidence, pending profile change requests, workflow progress/versioning, minimal provisioning records, and necessary protected OAuth/session state.

# Google is authoritative for Workspace users and administrative authority

This application serves one nonprofit's Google Workspace organization. Use Google-backed sign-in for existing Workspace users, Google Workspace administrative privileges for management authorization, and Google Workspace as the source of truth for existing user profiles and group membership, rather than maintaining parallel application-owned profiles or administrator roles.

The application stores signup requests separately because applicants do not yet have managed accounts. Signup uses verified contact email without requiring a personal Google account or an applicant dashboard. Workspace users may edit only their own permitted contact information; Workspace email, organizational assignments, group membership, account status, and security settings remain administrator-controlled. Administrators manage direct Workspace-user group membership, including member, manager, and owner roles; group roles alone do not grant application administration.

Suspension is the normal offboarding action. Deletion is a distinct, explicitly confirmed action after an administrator has resolved data disposition in Google's Admin console. Account handover uses the Admin console's existing-user password reset and email flow, with a required password change, rather than emailing a plaintext password.

Unreviewed signup requests expire after 30 days. Rejected applicant profiles are deleted after outcome notification; successful applicant form data is removed after provisioning and handover. Retain only a minimal operational record identifying the resulting Google account and approving administrator. Email verification evidence and pending workflow data may live in the application without becoming a second source of truth for the current Workspace profile.

PUT https://admin.googleapis.com/admin/directory/v1/users/userKey Both the request and response body contain an instance of
[User](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users#User). However, the Directory API supports
[patch semantics](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/v1/guides/performance#patch), so you only need to submit the updated fields in your request. Note: For repeating fields that contain arrays, like emails , individual items in the array can't be patched piecemeal; the field must be supplied in the request body with the desired values for all items, otherwise null items are cleared and other items might be unintentionally added or updated.

### Sample request

In the example below, the user's givenName was "Elizabeth" when the user account was created, and only a work email address was provided. { "name": { "givenName": "Elizabeth", "familyName": "Smith" }, "emails": [ { "address": "liz@example.com", "type": "work", "primary": true } ] } The following request updates givenName from "Elizabeth" to "Liz", and also adds a home email address. Note that both email addresses are provided fully because the field is an array. PUT https://admin.googleapis.com/admin/directory/v1/users/liz@example.com { "name": { "givenName": "Liz", }, "emails": [ { "address": "liz@example.com", "type": "work", "primary": true }, { "address": "liz@home.com", "type": "home" } ] } A successful response returns an
[HTTP 200 status code](http://wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_HTTP_status_codes)and a
[User](https://developers.google.com/workspace/admin/directory/reference/rest/v1/users#resource:-user)resource with the updated fields. Be aware of the following when updating a user's account name:

* Renaming a user account changes the user's primary email address and the domain used when retrieving this user's information. Before renaming a user, we recommend that you sign out the user from all browser sessions and services.
* The process of renaming a user account can take up to 10 minutes to propagate across all services.
* When you rename a user, the old user name is retained as an alias to ensure continuous mail delivery in the case of email forwarding settings, and is not available as a new user name.
* In general, we also recommend not using the user email address as a key for persistent data because the email address is subject to change.
* For a full list of the effects of renaming a user across Google Workspace apps, see the
[Admin help center](https://support.google.com/a/answer/2622985).

"}]}

# Google (/docs/authentication/google)

Google provider setup and usage.



<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Get your Google credentials [#get-your-google-credentials]

    To use Google as a social provider, you need to get your Google credentials. You can get them by creating a new project in the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/dashboard).

    In the Google Cloud Console > Credentials > Authorized redirect URIs, make sure to set the redirect URL to `http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google` for local development. For production, make sure to set the redirect URL as your application domain, e.g. `https://example.com/api/auth/callback/google`. If you change the base path of the auth routes, you should update the redirect URL accordingly.

    <Callout type="info">
      **Creating Your Google OAuth Credentials**

      If you haven't created OAuth credentials yet, follow these step-by-step instructions:

      1. Open **Google Cloud Console** → **APIs & Services** → **Credentials**
      2. Click **Create Credentials** → **OAuth client ID**
      3. Choose **Web application**
      4. Add your redirect URIs:
         * `http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google` (for local development)
         * `https://your-domain.com/api/auth/callback/google` (for production)
      5. Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** into your environment variables

      These steps avoid common issues such as `redirect_uri_mismatch`.
    </Callout>
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Configure the provider [#configure-the-provider]

    To configure the provider, you need to pass the `clientId` and `clientSecret` to `socialProviders.google` in your auth configuration.

    ```ts title="auth.ts"
    import { betterAuth } from "better-auth"

    export const auth = betterAuth({
        baseURL: process.env.BETTER_AUTH_URL, // [!code highlight]
        socialProviders: {
            google: { // [!code highlight]
                clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string, // [!code highlight]
                clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string, // [!code highlight]
            }, // [!code highlight]
        },
    })
    ```

    <Callout type="warn">
      **Important: Set Your Base URL**

      You must configure the `baseURL` to avoid `redirect_uri_mismatch` errors. Better Auth uses this to construct the OAuth callback URL sent to Google.

      **Option 1: Environment Variable (Recommended)**

      Add to your `.env` file:

      ```dotenv
      BETTER_AUTH_URL=https://your-domain.com
      ```

      **Option 2: Explicit Configuration**

      Pass `baseURL` directly in the auth config as shown above.
      Without this, the callback URL may default to `localhost`, causing Google OAuth to fail in production.
    </Callout>
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Usage [#usage]

### Sign In with Google [#sign-in-with-google]

To sign in with Google, you can use the `signIn.social` function provided by the client. The `signIn` function takes an object with the following properties:

* `provider`: The provider to use. It should be set to `google`.

```ts title="auth-client.ts"  /
import { createAuthClient } from "better-auth/client";
const authClient = createAuthClient();

const signIn = async () => {
  const data = await authClient.signIn.social({
    provider: "google",
  });
};
```

### Sign In with Google With ID Token [#sign-in-with-google-with-id-token]

To sign in with Google using the ID Token, you can use the `signIn.social` function to pass the ID Token.

This is useful when you have the ID Token from Google on the client-side and want to use it to sign in on the server.

<Callout>
  If ID token is provided no redirection will happen, and the user will be
  signed in directly.
</Callout>

```ts title="auth-client.ts"
const data = await authClient.signIn.social({
    provider: "google",
    idToken: {
        token: // Google ID Token,
        accessToken: // Google Access Token
    }
})
```

<Callout>
  If you want to use google one tap, you can use the [One Tap
  Plugin](/docs/plugins/one-tap) guide.
</Callout>

### Cross-Platform Sign In (Web, iOS, Android) [#cross-platform-sign-in-web-ios-android]

Google issues a separate Client ID per platform in the same Google Cloud project. Pass an array to `clientId` to accept ID tokens from any of them. See [clientId](/docs/concepts/oauth#clientid) for the shared provider-option semantics.

```ts title="auth.ts"
socialProviders: {
    google: {
        clientId: [ // [!code highlight]
            process.env.GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID as string, // [!code highlight]
            process.env.GOOGLE_IOS_CLIENT_ID as string, // [!code highlight]
            process.env.GOOGLE_ANDROID_CLIENT_ID as string, // [!code highlight]
        ], // [!code highlight]
        clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
    },
}
```

Your mobile app signs in with the native Google SDK and forwards the ID token:

```ts title="Mobile app"
const { idToken, accessToken } = await GoogleSignin.signIn();

await authClient.signIn.social({
    provider: "google",
    idToken: { token: idToken, accessToken },
});
```

<Callout type="info">
  The array only expands ID token audience verification. The authorization code flow still uses the first entry paired with the single `clientSecret` and `redirectURI`, so those cannot vary per platform within one provider block.
</Callout>

### Restrict Sign-In to Google Workspace [#restrict-sign-in-to-google-workspace]

Set `hd` on the Google provider to require a verified Google Workspace hosted-domain claim. Google also receives this value as an account-selection hint, but Better Auth enforces the returned ID token/profile claim after Google signs the response.

```ts title="auth.ts"
socialProviders: {
    google: {
        clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string,
        clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
        hd: "company.com", // [!code highlight]
    },
}
```

Set `hd: "*"` to allow any Google Workspace hosted domain. Tokens with no `hd` claim are rejected whenever `hd` is configured.

<Callout type="warn">
  A custom `getUserInfo` callback replaces Google's built-in callback-path `hd`
  check. Validate the claim from a trusted provider response and return `null`
  when it is missing or does not match. Direct ID-token sign-in follows the
  provider's ID-token verification path, while Google One Tap enforces the
  configured `hd` separately.
</Callout>

### Always ask to select an account [#always-ask-to-select-an-account]

If you want to always ask the user to select an account, you pass the `prompt` parameter to the provider, setting it to `select_account`.

```ts
socialProviders: {
    google: {
        prompt: "select_account", // [!code highlight]
        clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string,
        clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
    },
}
```

### Requesting Additional Google Scopes [#requesting-additional-google-scopes]

If your application needs additional Google scopes after the user has already signed up (e.g., for Google Drive, Gmail, or other Google services), you can request them using the `linkSocial` method with the same Google provider.

```tsx title="auth-client.ts"
const requestGoogleDriveAccess = async () => {
  await authClient.linkSocial({
    provider: "google",
    scopes: ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file"],
  });
};

// Example usage in a React component
return (
  <button onClick={requestGoogleDriveAccess}>
    Add Google Drive Permissions
  </button>
);
```

This will trigger a new OAuth flow that requests the additional scopes. After completion, your account will have the new scope in the database, and the access token will give you access to the requested Google APIs.

<Callout>
  Ensure you're using Better Auth version 1.2.7 or later to avoid "Social
  account already linked" errors when requesting additional scopes from the same
  provider.
</Callout>

### Disable incremental authorization [#disable-incremental-authorization]

By default, Better Auth sends `include_granted_scopes=true` to Google's authorization endpoint so newly issued access tokens cover scopes from prior grants in addition to the ones requested for the current flow. Set `includeGrantedScopes: false` if each OAuth flow should request only its own scopes.

```ts
socialProviders: {
    google: {
        clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string,
        clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
        includeGrantedScopes: false, // [!code highlight]
    },
}
```

Call-time `additionalParams.include_granted_scopes` still follows the general OAuth parameter precedence rules and can override this provider default for a single flow.

See Google's [Incremental authorization](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server#incrementalAuth) docs for the underlying parameter behavior.

### Always get refresh token [#always-get-refresh-token]

Google only issues a refresh token the first time a user consents to your app.
If the user has already authorized your app, subsequent OAuth flows will only return an access token, not a refresh token.

To always get a refresh token, you can set the `accessType` to `offline`, and `prompt` to `select_account consent` in the provider options.

```ts
socialProviders: {
    google: {
        clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID as string,
        clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET as string,
        accessType: "offline", // [!code highlight]
        prompt: "select_account consent", // [!code highlight]
    },
}
```

<Callout>
  **Revoking Access:** If you want to get a new refresh token for a user who has
  already authorized your app, you must have them revoke your app's access in
  their Google account settings, then re-authorize.
</Callout>

### Restricting to a Google Workspace domain [#restricting-to-a-google-workspace-domain]

To limit sign-in to accounts in a specific Google Workspace domain, forward the
`hd` parameter on the call. This mirrors Google's `hd` authorization-URL
parameter and is resolved per request:

```ts
await authClient.signIn.social({
  provider: "google",
  additionalParams: { hd: "example.com" },
});
```

You can also set `hd` at the provider config level if the restriction is static
for your application.

Understanding authentication is crucial for protecting your application's data. This page will guide you through what React and Next.js features to use to implement auth.

Before starting, it helps to break down the process into three concepts:

1. **[Authentication](#authentication)**: Verifies if the user is who they say they are. It requires the user to prove their identity with something they have, such as a username and password.
2. **[Session Management](#session-management)**: Tracks the user's auth state across requests.
3. **[Authorization](#authorization)**: Decides what routes and data the user can access.

This diagram shows the authentication flow using React and Next.js features:

You can, however, opt into caching for `GET` methods. Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached. To cache a `GET` method, use a [route config option](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components#dynamic) such as `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` in your Route Handler file. 52: 53: ```ts filename="app/items/route.ts" switcher 54: export const dynamic = 'force-static' 55: 56: export async function GET() { 57: const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', { 58: headers: { 59: 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 60: 'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY, 61: }, 62: }) 63: const data = await res.json() 64: 65: return Response.json({ data }) 66: } 67: ``` 68: 69: ```js filename="app/items/route.js" switcher 70: export const dynamic = 'force-static' 71: 72: export async function GET() { 73: const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', { 74: headers: { 75: 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 76: 'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY, 77: }, 78: }) 79: const data = await res.json() 80: 81: return Response.json({ data }) 82: } 83: ``` 84: 85: > **Good to know**: Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached, even if they are placed alongside a `GET` method that is cached, in the same file. 86: 87: #### With Cache Components 88: 89: When [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) is enabled, `GET` Route Handlers follow the same model as normal UI routes in your application. ## Quickstart

The fastest way to get started is to use `create-next-app` with the [with-playwright example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/with-playwright). This will create a Next.js project complete with Playwright configured.

pnpm create next-app --example with-playwright with-playwright-app

```bash package="npm"

# Drizzle ORM Adapter (/docs/adapters/drizzle)

Integrate Better Auth with Drizzle ORM.



Drizzle ORM is a powerful and flexible ORM for Node.js and TypeScript. It provides a simple and intuitive API for working with databases, and supports a wide range of databases including MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and more.

Before getting started, make sure you have Drizzle installed and configured. For more information, see [Drizzle Documentation](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/overview/)

## Installation [#installation]

To use the Drizzle adapter, you need to install the `@better-auth/drizzle-adapter` package:

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm" groupId="persist-install">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">
      npm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">
      pnpm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">
      yarn
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
      bun
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">
    ```bash
    npm install @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">
    ```bash
    pnpm add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="yarn">
    ```bash
    yarn add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">
    ```bash
    bun add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

## Example Usage [#example-usage]

You can use the Drizzle adapter to connect to your database as follows.

```ts title="auth.ts"
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";
import { drizzleAdapter } from "@better-auth/drizzle-adapter";
import { db } from "./database.ts";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, { // [!code highlight]
    provider: "sqlite", // or "pg" or "mysql" // [!code highlight]
  }), // [!code highlight]
  //... the rest of your config
});
```

## Schema generation & migration [#schema-generation--migration]

The [Better Auth CLI](/docs/concepts/cli) allows you to generate or migrate
your database schema based on your Better Auth configuration and plugins.

To generate the schema required by Better Auth, run the following command:

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm" groupId="persist-install">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">
      npm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">
      pnpm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">
      yarn
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
      bun
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">
    ```bash
    npx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">
    ```bash
    pnpm dlx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="yarn">
    ```bash
    yarn dlx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">
    ```bash
    bun x auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

To generate and apply the migration, run the following commands:

<Tabs items="["generate", "migrate"]">
  <Tab value="generate">
    <CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm" groupId="persist-install">
      <CodeBlockTabsList>
        <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">

        </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

        <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">

        <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">

        <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
          bun
        </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

        npx drizzle-kit generate # generate the migration file

    </CodeBlockTabs>

## Joins [#joins]

Database joins are useful when Better-Auth needs to fetch related data from multiple tables in a single query.
Endpoints like `/get-session`, `/get-full-organization` and many others benefit greatly from this feature,
seeing upwards of 2x to 3x performance improvements depending on database latency.

The Drizzle adapter supports joins out of the box since version `1.4.0`.
To enable this feature, set `advanced.database.joins` to `true` in your auth configuration.

```ts title="auth.ts"
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  advanced: {
    database: {
      joins: true,
    },
  },
});
```

<Callout type="warn">
  Please make sure that your Drizzle schema has the necessary relations defined.
  If you do not see any relations in your Drizzle schema, you can manually add them using the [`relation`](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations) drizzle-orm function
  or run our latest CLI version `npx auth@latest generate` to generate a new Drizzle schema with the relations.

  Additionally, you're required to pass each [relation](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations) through the drizzle adapter schema object.
</Callout>

When a table has multiple foreign keys to the same table, each relation pair
must use a matching [`relationName`](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations#disambiguating-relations).
The CLI generates these names automatically. If you generated your schema with
an older CLI, regenerate it or add matching names to both sides.

The `relationName` prefix follows your table naming: with `usePlural: true` it
is plural (`tests_userId`), otherwise singular (`test_userId`). Keep both sides
identical.

```ts title="schema.ts"
export const usersRelations = relations(users, ({ many }) => ({
  testsByUserId: many(tests, { relationName: "tests_userId" }),
  testsByManagerId: many(tests, { relationName: "tests_managerId" }),
}));

export const testsRelations = relations(tests, ({ one }) => ({
  user: one(users, {
    fields: [tests.userId],
    references: [users.id],
    relationName: "tests_userId",
  }),
  manager: one(users, {
    fields: [tests.managerId],
    references: [users.id],
    relationName: "tests_managerId",
  }),
}));
```

Do not keep both singular and plural aliases for the same foreign key (for
example, both `user` and `users`). Drizzle treats those as separate relations
and cannot infer which reverse relation a join should use.

## Modifying Table Names [#modifying-table-names]

The Drizzle adapter expects the schema you define to match the table names. For example, if your Drizzle schema maps the `user` table to `users`, you need to manually pass the schema and map it to the user table.

```ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";
import { db } from "./drizzle";
import { drizzleAdapter } from "@better-auth/drizzle-adapter";
import { schema } from "./schema";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
    provider: "sqlite", // or "pg" or "mysql"
    schema: { // [!code highlight]
      ...schema, // [!code highlight]
      user: schema.users, // [!code highlight]
    }, // [!code highlight]
  }),
});
```

You can either modify the provided schema values like the example above,
or you can mutate the auth config's `modelName` property directly.
For example:

```ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
    provider: "sqlite", // or "pg" or "mysql"
    schema,
  }),
  user: {
    modelName: "users", // [!code highlight]
  }
});
```

## Modifying Field Names [#modifying-field-names]

We map field names based on property you passed to your Drizzle schema.
For example, if you want to modify the `email` field to `email_address`,
you simply need to change the Drizzle schema to:

```ts
export const user = mysqlTable("user", {
  // Changed field name without changing the schema property name
  // This allows drizzle & better-auth to still use the original field name,
  // while your DB uses the modified field name
  email: varchar("email_address", { length: 255 }).notNull().unique(), // [!code highlight]
  // ... others
});
```

You can either modify the Drizzle schema like the example above,
or you can mutate the auth config's `fields` property directly.
For example:

```ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
    provider: "sqlite", // or "pg" or "mysql"
    schema,
  }),
  user: {
    fields: {
      email: "email_address", // [!code highlight]
    }
  }
});
```

## Using Plural Table Names [#using-plural-table-names]

If all your tables are using plural form, you can just pass the `usePlural` option:

```ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
    ...
    usePlural: true, // [!code highlight]
  }),
});
```

## Custom Schema namespace [#custom-schema-namespace]

If you're using PostgreSQL and you want to generate the schema with a custom schema namespace,
you can pass the `schemaName` option to the Drizzle adapter.

```ts
export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
    provider: "pg",
    schemaName: "auth", // [!code highlight]
  }),
});
```

Then when using the Better Auth CLI, it will generate the schema that looks something like this:

```bash
npx auth@latest generate
```

```ts
export const authSchema = pgSchema("auth");

export const user = authSchema.table("user", {...});
export const session = authSchema.table("session", {...});
```

The `schemaName` option is also supported by the
`@better-auth/drizzle-adapter/relations-v2` adapter described below.

## Drizzle Relations v2 [#drizzle-relations-v2]

The default Drizzle adapter uses Relations v1. For Drizzle Relations v2, use
`@better-auth/drizzle-adapter/relations-v2`.

Install the adapter:

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm" groupId="persist-install">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">
      npm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">
      pnpm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">
      yarn
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
      bun
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">
    ```bash
    npm install @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">
    ```bash
    pnpm add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="yarn">
    ```bash
    yarn add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">
    ```bash
    bun add @better-auth/drizzle-adapter
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

Configure Better Auth with the v2 adapter and your auth schema:

```ts title="auth.ts"
import { betterAuth } from 'better-auth';
import { drizzleAdapter } from '@better-auth/drizzle-adapter/relations-v2'; // [!code highlight]
import { db } from './db.ts';
import * as schema from './auth-schema.ts';

export const auth = betterAuth({
	database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
		provider: 'sqlite', // or "pg" or "mysql"
		schema, // [!code highlight]
	}),
	//... the rest of your config
});
```

Then regenerate your schema using the Better Auth CLI:

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="npm" groupId="persist-install">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">
      npm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">
      pnpm
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="yarn">
      yarn
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>

    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">
      bun
    </CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>

  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">
    ```bash
    npx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">
    ```bash
    pnpm dlx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="yarn">
    ```bash
    yarn dlx auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>

  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">
    ```bash
    bun x auth@latest generate
    ```
  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

<Callout type="info">
  You do not need to run database migrations when upgrading to Relations v2. The
  database structure remains the same - only the relation definitions change.
  The schema generator will output the new v2 format automatically.
</Callout>

Merge the generated auth relations after your app's relations in your existing
Drizzle configuration:

```ts title="db.ts"
import { authRelations } from './auth-schema.ts';
import { relations } from './app-schema.ts';

export const db = drizzle({
	client,
	relations: { ...relations, ...authRelations }, // [!code highlight]
});
```

<Callout type="info">
  `defineRelationsPart` is a partial relation definition that must be spread
  after full `defineRelations` entries. See the
  [Drizzle docs on relation parts](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/relations-v2#relations-parts)
  for details.
</Callout>

## Additional Information [#additional-information]

* If you're looking for performance improvements or tips, take a look at our guide to <Link href="/docs/guides/optimizing-for-performance">performance optimizations</Link>.

parts.text:
## Plan for issue #2

Implement **Google Workspace sign-in and own-profile viewing** using Better Auth social sign-on.

### 1. Authentication and persistence
- Configure Better Auth with Google, Drizzle, and Postgres.
- Request OpenID identity scopes plus `admin.directory.user.readonly`, with offline access for refresh.
- Validate token signature, issuer, audience, expiry, verified email, and the configured Workspace `hd` claim. Preserve state/PKCE and applicable nonce protections.
- Disable direct browser-supplied ID-token sign-in and account linking.
- Encrypt persisted OAuth credentials. Keep token retrieval and refresh endpoints inaccessible over HTTP while using their server-side APIs.
- Store only required authentication/session data and a stable Directory identity binding.

**Important finding:** Better Auth’s inspected Google callback decodes the ID token; I’ll explicitly verify it cryptographically before accepting the identity.

### 2. Stable identity and protected access
- Resolve the Directory ID server-side from fresh, verified Google identity information.
- Persist the binding separately from Google’s OpenID `sub`; never assume the two identifiers are equal.
- Enforce unique bindings in Postgres and reject conflicting resolutions rather than switching identities.
- Use the stored Directory ID for subsequent reads, including after primary-email changes.
- Require a successful fresh Directory lookup using the signed-in user’s grant and `viewType=domain_public`.
- Deny access on missing/hidden profiles, credential rejection, identity mismatch, or lookup failure. Provide clear retry or reconnection outcomes.

### 3. Browser journey
Replace the scaffold with:
- Google sign-in.
- A protected profile showing current permitted name, Workspace email, contact emails, and phones.
- “Unavailable” for omitted contact fields.
- Sign-out, loading, error, and reconnection states.

Reuse the existing shadcn button and Tailwind styling.

### 4. Behavior checks
Add Playwright tests against the running application and an isolated real Postgres database using actual Drizzle migrations. Control Google responses at external network boundaries, keeping production authentication enforcement active.

Cover:
- Sign-in, fresh profile changes, sign-out, and session revocation.
- Invalid tokens, wrong/personal organizations, state tampering/replay, and consent denial.
- Expired/revoked credentials and refresh failure.
- Hidden/deleted profiles and Directory failures.
- Email changes, identity collisions, concurrent binding attempts, and browser-controlled target IDs.
- Credentials remaining server-side.

Docker is installed but stopped, and local Postgres is unavailable. The database test environment must be started during implementation. Live-tenant checks also require Workspace credentials and dedicated test accounts.

### 5. Delivery
Create the required `.worktrees` worktree and GitHub stack, commit small functional changes, run typechecking, lint, formatting, build, and browser checks, then perform the required standards/spec review. Submit the stack and update issue #2 with results and the PR link.

Configuration will use `DATABASE_URL`, `BETTER_AUTH_URL`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, and `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_DOMAIN`.

No implementation changes have been made while plan mode is active.

   6. Add the stack to github.

<skill_content name="tdd">
# Skill: tdd

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams: where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

1: # When to Mock
2: 
3: Mock at **system boundaries** only:
4: 
5: - External APIs (payment, email, etc.)
6: - Databases (sometimes - prefer test DB)
7: - Time/randomness
8: - File system (sometimes)
9: 
10: Don't mock:
11: 
12: - Your own classes/modules
13: - Internal collaborators
14: - Anything you control
15: 
16: ## Designing for Mockability
17: 
18: At system boundaries, design interfaces that are easy to mock:
19: 
20: **1. Use dependency injection**
21: 
22: Pass external dependencies in rather than creating them internally:
23: 
24: ```typescript
25: // Easy to mock
26: function processPayment(order, paymentClient) {
27:   return paymentClient.charge(order.total);
28: }
29: 
30: // Hard to mock
31: function processPayment(order) {
32:   const client = new StripeClient(process.env.STRIPE_KEY);
33:   return client.charge(order.total);
34: }
35: ```
36: 
37: **2. Prefer SDK-style interfaces over generic fetchers**
38: 
39: Create specific functions for each external operation instead of one generic function with conditional logic:
40: 
41: ```typescript
42: // GOOD: Each function is independently mockable
43: const api = {
44:   getUser: (id) => fetch(`/users/${id}`),
45:   getOrders: (userId) => fetch(`/users/${userId}/orders`),
46:   createOrder: (data) => fetch('/orders', { method: 'POST', body: data }),
47: };
48: 
49: // BAD: Mocking requires conditional logic inside the mock
50: const api = {
51:   fetch: (endpoint, options) => fetch(endpoint, options),
52: };
53: ```
54: 
55: The SDK approach means:
56: - Each mock returns one specific shape
57: - No conditional logic in test setup
58: - Easier to see which endpoints a test exercises
59: - Type safety per endpoint

(End of file - total 59 lines)
</content>

+# Binden
+
+Google Workspace sign-in and current own-profile viewing, built with Next.js,
+Better Auth social sign-on, shadcn/Tailwind, and Drizzle/Postgres.
+
+## Setup
+
+1. Run `pnpm install` and copy `.env.example` to `.env.local`.
+2. Set `DATABASE_URL` to your Neon pooled Postgres connection URL, with TLS enabled.
+   The application runs in the Node.js runtime and uses a small, idle-expiring
+   `pg` pool, which also supports ordinary Postgres for development.
+3. Generate `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` with `openssl rand -base64 32`. Keep it stable:
+   it protects sessions and encrypts the stored OAuth access/refresh tokens.
+4. Set `BETTER_AUTH_URL` to the application origin (HTTPS in production),
+   `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, and `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_DOMAIN` to
+   the organization's Google hosted-domain claim. These are server-only values.
+5. Enable the Admin SDK API in your Google Cloud project. Configure an internal
+   OAuth web client for the Workspace organization. Add
+   `<BETTER_AUTH_URL>/api/auth/callback/google` to its authorized redirect URIs.
+   Request `openid`, `email`, `profile`, and
+   `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.directory.user.readonly`; users must
+   grant the Directory permission. Workspace policy must allow the application.
+6. Enable administrator-managed Directory/contact sharing and ensure managed
+   users are visible. Only fields returned by `domain_public` can be displayed.
+7. Apply committed migrations with `DATABASE_URL=… pnpm db:migrate`, then run
+   `pnpm dev`. Drizzle CLI loads `.env`; alternatively export `DATABASE_URL`
+   explicitly. Next.js loads `.env.local` for development, build, and start.
+
+The app asks for offline access and consent to obtain a refresh token. Revoked
+connections require sign-in again. Better Auth's browser-facing routes are
+limited to social sign-in, the Google callback, and sign-out. OAuth tokens are
+never returned to the browser. Direct ID-token sign-in and account linking are
+disabled. This authorization-code flow uses browser-bound, single-use database
+state and PKCE; it does not request an OIDC nonce. Callback ID tokens are still
+cryptographically checked for signature, issuer, audience, age/expiry, and the
+Workspace claim before creating a session.
+
+Google's subject and Directory ID are bound separately. Fresh UserInfo provides
+the initial lookup email; after binding, every lookup uses the stable Directory
+ID. Mutable emails are consistency checks, not identity keys. Better Auth's
+required name/email fields contain inert authentication metadata, not a cached
+Workspace profile. ID tokens are discarded after verification. No local roles,
+authoritative profile copies, shared reader credentials, or admin-view fallback
+are used.
+
+## Checks
+
+```bash
+pnpm typecheck
+pnpm lint
+pnpm format:check
+pnpm build
+```
+
+Build requires the configuration above. Browser checks run the production build
+with isolated, test-only configuration and controlled Google network responses:
+
+```bash
+pnpm exec playwright install chromium
+TEST_DATABASE_URL=REDACTED pnpm test:e2e
+```
+
+Use a disposable Postgres instance with `CREATE DATABASE` permission. The
+launcher creates a randomly named database, applies the real Drizzle migrations,
+and drops it at teardown; it never uses the application's `DATABASE_URL`.
+Ports 3100 and 3101 must be available. `E2E_DEV=1` uses Next's development server
+for test-first iteration. The test launcher alone loads the Google network
+fixture: production code has no authentication bypass or test-mode provider.
+
+## Live Workspace verification
+
+Simulated Google responses do not establish tenant behavior. With a dedicated
+managed test account, verify sign-in, profile visibility, Google-side changes,
+primary-email rename propagation, sign-out, and revocation/reconnection. Keep an
+existing application session while hiding, suspending, and deleting that account,
+then reload the profile. Record when Google rejects the credentials or Directory
+lookup. Access requires a successful current lookup, but Google credential and
+Directory propagation mean this is **not instantaneous suspension detection**.
+No administrator-only suspended/status fields are requested.
*** End Patch
